title: The Supreme Court’s mail-ballot rebuke of Trump wasn’t just a win for Democrats | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The reactions to the US Supreme Courtputting an endto President Donald Trump’sefforts to significantly restrict mail ballotsin the 2026 midterm elections were about what you’d expect.

It was largely Democrats, whose voters tend to avail themselves of mail voting more than Republicans do, who cheered the ruling. Trump, who has made no secret that he views his proposed election changes as helping Republicans,assailed it.

But it’s not totally clear that the restrictions would have harmed Democrats much, if at all, more than Republicans.

Indeed, the win in the Supreme Court ruling might be more for democracy than for Democrats.

APostal Service whistleblowerrecently warned that the sweeping newsystem for verifying mail ballotswas prone to errors and could lead to mass disenfranchisement of votes. And that would seem primed to hurt Democrats.

But while Democrats vote by mail more, multiple estimates show that gapnarrowed somewhat between 2020 and 2024. Amid expanded mail voting during the Covid pandemic in 2020, the Pew Research Center found that 58% of validated voters who voted Democratic said theyvoted by mail, while just 32% of Republican voters did. By 2024, the numbers were43% for Democratic voters and 25% for Republican ones.

But the option is arguably more important for older and rural voters who live further from polling places, and those people tend to be more Republican than Democratic.

ACBS News pollamong likely voters released this weekend showed mail and absentee ballot intentions looked a lot like the 2024 election, with 38% of Democrats planning to vote that way, compared to 22% of Republicans.

But Democrats were much more likely to say they intended to return their mail or absentee ballots through drop boxes rather than the mail service (40% of them) than Republicans were (15%).

All told, the poll found around 1in 5 Democrats planned to vote by mail or absenteeandreturn their ballot through the mail service — only a little more than Republicans.

Longtime Republican elections lawyer Ben Ginsberg, who has sharply criticized Trump’s efforts to meddle in US elections and his claims of widespread fraud, has suggested the president’s plans to change mail voting might actually have backfired on Republicans.

Ginsberg said that was not just because GOP voters are older and more rural, but also because they’re disproportionatelyless likely to turn out to votein elections that don’t feature Trump on the ballot.

“Thanks to Donald Trump, there are many more low-propensity voters in the Republican Party,” Ginsberg said on CNN’s “The Source with Kaitlan Collins” last month. “And Republican operatives in the states know that putting up those barriers to that part of the Republican base makes Republican turnout less likely.”

Ginsberg called it a “flawed political strategy wrapped in a rather vocally charged policy.”

Polls have also shown that Republican voters aresignificantly less enthusiasticabout voting in the 2026 midterms than Democrats.

In other words, it’s too simple to just look at which side votes by mail more. To really gauge the impact of Trump’s changes and the ruling blocking them, you have to look at who might be dissuaded from voting at all or not have a ballot returned because of the restrictions.

The USPS whistleblower claimed that if there was just one discrepancy between voter lists submitted by state elections officials and the mail ballots they send out, entire batches of tens of thousands of ballots could be held up.

If mail ballots being sent to voters were held up because of that potential mass disruption, it would matter which party’s voters are more likely to use other avenues to vote or might not vote at all.

Regardless of whose voters the change might ultimately have hurt more, though, there were certainly plenty of ways the rushed restrictions could have created a debacle or threatened free and fair elections.

Trump, after all, has shown he’s plenty willing to do whatever it takes to win and has frequently flirted withmeddling in how elections are run.

And even if that wasn’t the administration’s intention, allowing the changes so late in the game could have opened up a Pandora’s box. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, said in his concurrence that he was open to the rule changes being legal, but that election officials did “not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule.”

All of which might help explain why it wasn’tonlyDemocrats who challenged the changes; so too didsome Republican secretaries of state.
